## 1. Identification Strategy
- Strategy: Randomized controlled field experiment (correspondence study), analyzed with within-job-ad comparisons.
- Justification: Names that signal perceived race are randomly assigned to otherwise identical resumes. Randomization ensures that, in expectation, resumes with African-American-sounding names and White-sounding names are identical on all observed and unobserved dimensions except the perceived race signal. Multiple resumes per job ad allow job-ad fixed effects to purge all job-level heterogeneity in callback propensity and increase precision. The estimand is the intent-to-treat effect of being perceived as African-American on the probability of receiving a callback.

## 2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable: Indicator equal to 1 if the resume was assigned an African-American-sounding first name; 0 if assigned a White-sounding first name.
- Control group: Resumes with White-sounding names.
- Secondary randomized factor: Resume quality (high vs. low). We will estimate its main effect and its interaction with the race signal to test whether higher qualifications attenuate discrimination.
- Treatment timing / event date: One-shot at the time the resume is sent. No staggered timing is relevant.
- RDD: Not applicable.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- A1. Random assignment: Name type is randomly assigned and independent of potential callbacks conditional on job ad. Plausible given the design; can be verified with balance tests on resume characteristics by treatment.
- A2. Stable unit treatment value (no interference): The callback outcome for a resume depends only on its own assigned name/quality and not on the names/qualities of other resumes sent to the same ad. Plausibility is moderate; employers may face capacity constraints or notice multiple similar applicants. Estimation with job-ad fixed effects and design choices (distinct resumes, limited saturation per ad) help, and we will do robustness restricting to ads with exactly one Black- and one White-named resume.
- A3. Consistent outcome measurement and blinding: Callbacks are recorded without knowledge of treatment or with procedures that do not differentially misclassify outcomes by name type. Plausible with standardized tracking and researcher blinding to treatment at coding time; we can document procedures and run inter-coder reliability checks if applicable.
- A4. Excludability/construct validity: The “name treatment” affects callbacks primarily through perceived race rather than other traits (e.g., social class). This is the main construct validity concern. We mitigate by (i) using name lists with well-documented racial perceptions, (ii) balancing other resume features (address, education, etc.) and (iii) showing robustness across alternative name sets and controlling for name popularity or “Blackness probability.”
- A5. Correct inference: Errors are clustered at the job-ad (and, if identifiable, employer) level to reflect the assignment and within-ad correlation. We will also implement randomization inference as a robustness check.

## 4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
- Threat 1: Names may signal socioeconomic background, not only race.
  - Remedy: Use name lists validated to strongly signal race; show that effects are robust across multiple African-American and White name subsets; control for resume address characteristics with zip code fixed effects; include name fixed effects or controls for name frequency/“Blackness probability” from external data (e.g., birth records) in robustness checks; test for similar effects within narrow strata (e.g., same city, same zip, same school type).
- Threat 2: Within-ad interference or capacity constraints (SUTVA violations).
  - Remedy: Include job-ad fixed effects so identification is within ad; conduct robustness restricting to ads with exactly two resumes (one Black, one White) to emulate classic paired design; control for “ad saturation” by including number of resumes sent to that ad; test for sensitivity of estimates to excluding highly saturated ads.
- Threat 3: Differential measurement or detection by employers.
  - Remedy: Ensure resumes are distinct in layout and content (aside from treatment dimensions) to avoid detection; blind coders to treatment when recording callbacks; run a falsification test on impossible-to-be-affected fields (e.g., whether the ad phone number was reachable) and inter-coder agreement checks.

## 5. R Code Outline
Assumptions about variable names in the CSV (adjust as needed):
- callback: 1 if employer contacted applicant, 0 otherwise
- first_name: first name string
- black_name: 1 if name is African-American-sounding (if not present, we create from first_name)
- high_quality: 1 if high-quality resume
- ad_id: unique ID for job ad
- employer_id: firm identifier if available
- city, occupation, industry, eeo (equal opportunity employer indicator), zip, gender, years_exp, skills_count, certification_count

```r
# ------------- Setup -------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(modelsummary)
library(sandwich)

# ------------- Data loading -------------
df <- read_csv("resumes.csv")

# ------------- Treatment construction -------------
# If black_name not pre-computed, construct from name lists
if(!("black_name" %in% names(df))) {
  black_names <- c("Lakisha","Jamal","Tamika","Tyrone","Aisha","Jeron","Kenya","Latoya",
                   "Rasheed","Tawanda","Deshawn","Shaniqua") # extend as appropriate
  white_names <- c("Emily","Greg","Anne","Brad","Allison","Brett","Amanda","Jay",
                   "Jill","Neil","Meredith","Todd") # extend as appropriate
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(black_name = case_when(first_name %in% black_names ~ 1L,
                                  first_name %in% white_names ~ 0L,
                                  TRUE ~ NA_integer_))
}

# Keep observations with valid treatment assignment
df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(black_name))

# ------------- Optional: Balance checks -------------
# Check that randomized treatment is orthogonal to resume observables
balance_vars <- c("high_quality","gender","years_exp","skills_count","certification_count","zip","city","occupation","industry","eeo")
# Simple differences for numeric vars
df %>% 
  summarise(across(c(years_exp, skills_count, certification_count),
                   ~mean(.x[black_name==1], na.rm=TRUE) - mean(.x[black_name==0], na.rm=TRUE))) %>% print()

# Regression-based balance within ad fixed effects
bal_form <- as.formula(paste0("high_quality ~ black_name | ad_id"))
feols(bal_form, data=df, cluster=~ad_id) %>% summary()

# ------------- Main specification -------------
# LPM with job-ad fixed effects; cluster at ad level
main_form <- callback ~ black_name + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender + eeo
m1 <- feols(main_form | ad_id, data=df, cluster = ~ ad_id)
summary(m1)

# Add city x occupation fixed effects as controls (if desired)
m2 <- feols(callback ~ black_name + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender + eeo | ad_id + city^occupation,
            data=df, cluster = ~ ad_id)
summary(m2)

# ------------- Alternative GLM (logit) with ad FE -------------
m3 <- feglm(callback ~ black_name + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender + eeo | ad_id,
            data=df, family=binomial("logit"), cluster=~ad_id)
summary(m3)

# ------------- Robustness: Restrict to paired ads -------------
# Ads with at least one Black and one White resume
df_pair <- df %>% group_by(ad_id) %>%
  filter(n_distinct(black_name) == 2) %>% ungroup()

m_pair <- feols(callback ~ black_name + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender + eeo | ad_id,
                data=df_pair, cluster=~ad_id)
summary(m_pair)

# ------------- Robustness: Heterogeneity by EEO statement -------------
m_eeo <- feols(callback ~ black_name*eeo + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender | ad_id,
               data=df, cluster=~ad_id)
summary(m_eeo)

# ------------- Randomization inference (permutation within ad) -------------
set.seed(123)
B <- 1000
coef_dist <- numeric(B)

# Function to compute coefficient on black_name quickly
get_beta <- function(dat) {
  est <- feols(callback ~ black_name + high_quality + black_name:high_quality + gender + eeo | ad_id,
               data=dat, cluster=~ad_id, warn=FALSE, notes=FALSE)
  coef(est)["black_name"]
}

beta_hat <- get_beta(df)

for(b in 1:B){
  df_perm <- df %>%
    group_by(ad_id) %>%
    mutate(black_name = sample(black_name)) %>%
    ungroup()
  coef_dist[b] <- get_beta(df_perm)
}
ri_pval <- mean(abs(coef_dist) >= abs(beta_hat))
cat("Randomization-inference p-value for black_name:", ri_pval, "\n")

# ------------- Presentation -------------
modelsummary(list("FE LPM"=m1,"FE LPM + city x occ"=m2,"FE Logit"=m3,"Paired ads"=m_pair),
             gof_omit = "Adj|IC|Log|F",
             stars = TRUE)
```

Notes:
- The ad_id fixed effects make the comparison strictly within a job ad, improving precision.
- Cluster at ad_id because treatment is assigned within ads and outcomes are correlated within ads. If multiple ads can be linked to the same employer, report two-way clustered SEs (ad_id and employer_id) as a robustness check.
- The randomization inference block preserves the assignment structure within ad_id.

## 6. Expected Results
- Direction: Lower callback rates for resumes with African-American-sounding names.
- Magnitude: Prior from theory and prior literature suggests a meaningful but not enormous effect. A reasonable prior is a 2–6 percentage point lower callback probability (roughly a 20–40% relative reduction if baseline callback is around 10–15%). For the quality interaction, statistical discrimination predicts that higher resume quality could reduce the gap (i.e., a positive interaction term), though this attenuation may be modest.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RCT-focused)
- C1: Randomization implemented and balanced on observables within ads — 1
- C2: No interference/spillovers within ad (SUTVA) — 0
- C3: Outcome measured consistently and coders blinded to treatment — 1
- C4: Correct variance estimation aligned with assignment (clustered at ad; RI as robustness) — 1
- C5: Construct validity that name signals only race (not SES or other traits) — 0

Overall, internal validity is strong due to random assignment and within-ad comparisons. The main caveats are potential within-ad interference and the interpretation that the treatment captures perceived race rather than a bundle of correlated cues; we address these with design details and robustness analyses. External validity is limited to the sampled cities, occupations, and the early-2000s posting channels.
